meta: Dramas like Mystic Pop-up Bar: afterlife bureaucracy, grudges settled per episode, and warm supernatural comedy.
standfirst: Twelve episodes, a grudge-settling bar that operates inside people's dreams, and a five-hundred-year debt that gets paid off properly in the final stretch. The episodic cases are better than the mythology arc holding them together, and the comedy is broad without ever turning cruel. It is under-watched rather than disputed, and it is one of the easiest first Korean dramas to hand somebody: the hour-long episode is the only barrier and this show makes it vanish. Warm, silly, occasionally sad, and it sticks the goodbye.

picks.why: The same business model, with a bigger budget and better clothes. A supernatural establishment that serves the dead, a proprietor working off a debt measured in centuries, and one guest per episode with unfinished business. Difference: it is a melodrama at heart, glamorous and bittersweet, so it will actually make you cry where this one only gets close.

Supernatural civil service, case per episode, same clipboard energy. Same idea that the afterlife has departments, targets and a boss, and the same structure of a small team fixing one person's life per hour. Difference: the cases are suicide interventions at heavy 5, so it is far heavier and needs rationing, one episode a day rather than four in a row.

The other Korean myth comedy about a debt between a spirit and a woman who can see ghosts. Same appetite for folklore treated as contract law, same swings between slapstick and dread. Difference: twenty episodes, rough effects in places you will notice, and the first five are hard work before it becomes watchable.

Grudges resolved by supernatural authority, one case at a time. Same pleasure in a creative punishment fitted to the crime, and the same lead who is far more entertaining than the plot around her. Difference: the punishments are crueller, and a romance keeps interrupting the good part, which is Park Shin Hye.

The dead, the nearly dead, and one place they all pass through. Same premise of a threshold business staffed by somebody who knows more than the customers, same episodic reveals. Difference: eight quiet episodes that pretend to be horror for four, and the structural turn makes it grief rather than comedy.

An absurd premise played sincerely, which is this show's whole method. Same trust that a ridiculous setup can hold real feeling if the ensemble commits, comfort 5 and eight episodes with no filler. Difference: superheroes rather than spirits, no rules to learn, and the first two hours are the worst two.

against.title: The Uncanny Counter
against.why: Paired for the supernatural team and the food premises, and it is an action show. Fight choreography, a monster of the arc and a training-montage structure. What makes this one work is a bar, a grudge and a conversation, none of which survive the genre change.

against.title: Oh My Ghost
against.why: Recommended for the ghost comedy, and it runs on embarrassment plus a serial-killer subplot. Busier, hornier and much more plot-driven. The pleasure here is a found family settling somebody else's business and going home.

against.title: Bring It On, Ghost
against.why: The other spirit-and-mortal comedy, aimed at a younger room. It is a campus romance with exorcism attached, lighter on mythology and lighter on consequence. The five-hundred-year debt is the reason this show lands, and there is no equivalent weight there.
